title: Building a Research Operations Function
subtitle: From zero to a governed qualitative data repository

slides.title: Building a Research Operations Function
slides.standfirst: Founding the UX Research practice at Coupa, scaling it to 20+ product lines, and then solving the bottleneck that scale created: insight produced faster than the organisation could reuse it.

bullets.text: Director of User Experience Research and Design
One practitioner → a standing discipline → a governed repository
Headcount could not grow at the rate demand did

slides.notes: Two problems in sequence, and the second one only exists because the first was solved. Signal that structure early or the deck reads as two unrelated stories.

slides.title: An organisation deciding on assumption
slides.standfirst: Product managers and designers, no research function, and UX validation happening after build rather than before it.
slides.notes: Set the starting state honestly: not a bad organisation, an organisation with no mechanism.

slides.title: Customers were treated as interchangeable with end users
slides.standfirst: The people who sign the contract and the people who work in the product every day were the same population as far as prioritisation was concerned.

bullets.text: Feature requests arrived through commercial channels and were read as user needs.
Nobody was wrong on purpose — there was simply no counter-evidence available.
Demonstrating the difference required data, which required a function that did not yet exist.

slides.title: Three stages, each one making the next one possible

items.label: Establish the practice
items.detail: Executive conversation, the first UX survey, a Clarity research site, a Research Intake Form for PM, UserTesting licences

items.label: Scale the team
items.detail: Recruitment, onboarding, mentorship — and ownership moved off PMs onto trained researchers and designers

items.label: Fix the data architecture
items.detail: Dovetail budget secured, workspace and taxonomy designed, legacy projects migrated off Google Drive

figure.caption: Stage three is only a problem worth having because stages one and two worked

slides.notes: Each stage has a different kind of difficulty: political, managerial, architectural. Say which is which.

slides.title: The intake form was the real unlock
slides.standfirst: A research function with no intake process is a queue of favours. A formal Research Intake Form for the PM department turned requests into a triageable pipeline.

bullets.text: Initiated the case for a systematic research approach, not a headcount ask.
The homepage redesign survey — the proof of concept.
A dedicated Clarity site, so research had an address.
UserTesting licences as the standard evaluative platform.

figure.alt: Behaviour model used to frame the research practice
figure.caption: Framing the practice, not just the studies

slides.notes: Intake is unglamorous and it is the single highest-leverage artefact in the whole story. It converts demand into something you can say no to.

slides.title: Six to forty-plus
slides.standfirst: The UX organisation grew, and research ownership shifted off product managers and onto people trained to hold it.

items.label: Designers and researchers as the organisation scaled
Research initiatives delivered in a single year

slides.notes: Growth is the setup for the twist. More people producing more studies is precisely what broke the way findings were stored.

slides.title: The function worked. The knowledge did not accumulate.
slides.standfirst: Studies were run, but findings lived in Google Drive as unstructured documents owned by whoever ran the study.

bullets.text: Two researchers coding the same behaviour differently, permanently.
No way to ask a question across projects.
A project could not be handed from one researcher to another.
No quantitative reference against which to claim any product had improved.

callout.text: Insight was being produced faster than the organisation could reuse it. That is an information architecture problem wearing a headcount problem's clothes.

slides.notes: This slide is the pivot of the deck. Say the diagnosis sentence slowly — it is the line the rest of the work follows from.

slides.title: The team could not grow at the rate demand did, so throughput had to come from infrastructure

slides.notes: Every research leader hits this wall. The answer is almost never more researchers; it is fewer repeated motions per study.

slides.title: Securing budget for a category of tool the organisation had never funded
slides.standfirst: A research CMS has no obvious line item. The ROI case had to be made in operational efficiency, not in insight quality.

bullets.text: Dovetail, as the centralised research repository.
Reuse and cross-project analysis, quantified as researcher time.
25% improvement in research operational efficiency.

callout.text: The repository only produces value if the taxonomy is designed up front. Without a standardised structure, a shared repository is just a shared folder.

slides.notes: The callout is the sentence to remember. Most repository projects fail here, by buying the tool and deferring the schema.

slides.title: Recruitment, industrialised
slides.standfirst: Finding the right participant was the slowest step in every study, so it stopped being a per-study activity.

bullets.text: Salesforce, Metabase and Pendo filters to reach specific user profiles.
Large-scale email campaigns where a profile was broad.

slides.notes: Recruitment is where research operations either exists or does not. The tooling list is boring and it is the whole answer.

slides.title: Flexibility against structure
slides.standfirst: Governance that nobody follows is theatre; governance that constrains every study is friction. The taxonomy had to be strict where comparison mattered and open everywhere else.

slides.title: Scaling qualitative research is an information architecture problem
slides.standfirst: It arrives disguised as a headcount problem, and hiring against it makes the disguise more convincing — more researchers producing more unstructured documents faster.

callout.text: Can a researcher who has never met you pick up your project, find your data, and code the next interview the way you coded the last one? If not, you have a folder.

slides.notes: End on the test question. It is the most useful thing in the deck for anyone doing this work themselves.
